source.title: Evolutionary Algorithms in the Light of SGD: Limit Equivalence, Minima Flatness, and Transfer Learning
source.authors: Andrei Kucharavy; R. Guerraoui; Ljiljana Dolamic

record.file_problem: The supplied text includes the paper and appendix; some figure content is present only as captions or figure references.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies minima flatness, transfer learning, and noise robustness, but its experiments do not test any listed claim version: they do not measure same-distribution train–test gaps, random-label memorization, or the other version-specific outcomes. Its transfer task reveals occluded classes, so those results do not test the claim’s same-distribution generalization.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on overparameterization, dropout, batch size, and flat minima; those cited findings are not this study’s results. Its own MNIST results concern transfer to classes withheld during training and input corruption. Figure-only accuracy and robustness curves are not reconstructed as numerical values.
record.test_reason: The study measures normalized minima-flatness profiles, transfer to withheld MNIST classes, input-corruption robustness, and optimization progress. It does not measure the magnitude-aware sharpness–train/test-gap relationship in V7 or the comparisons required by V1–V6 and V8. Its argument against a broader flat-minima hypothesis therefore does not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. More precisely, the authors establish a mean-update equivalence under local smoothness, nonzero gradient, vanishing learning rate, and increasing population size. Their MNIST experiments suggest that flatter minima reflect redundant feature encoding and greater input-noise robustness, without an apparent advantage in withheld-class performance or transfer speed beyond known-class performance. Changes in flatness during transfer were inconclusive.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use MNIST class occlusion and input corruption to study minima flatness and transfer; they do not apply the interventions or measurements specified in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that minima flatness differs across the Robust Wide, Brittle Narrow, and Brittle Wide archetypes, which vary dropout, input dropout, latent maps, linear width, and batch size. The text also reports different noise robustness across flatness conditions; precise values are figure-only.

fits_no_version.finding: The flatter MNIST archetype did not perform better on withheld classes or learn them faster beyond its advantage on known classes, but was more resilient to input corruption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this MNIST class-transfer experiment, measured minima flatness accompanied corruption robustness without an apparent transfer-performance or transfer-speed advantage.

fits_no_version.finding: The base ConvNet reached validation error below 2% after 20 epochs and approximately 2.5% after 10 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The base MNIST ConvNet achieved the reported validation accuracy at the stated training durations.

fits_no_version.finding: The GO-EA proof of concept improved training accuracy from approximately 10% to 60% in about 800 sampling steps; SGD training progress was reported as a comparator.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A simple GO-EA can optimize this MNIST ConvNet using hyperparameters transferred from SGD.

record.problems: The transfer experiment withholds classes and therefore does not measure same-distribution held-out error. The text gives no numerical results for the archetype transfer and corruption comparisons; those are shown in figures. The GO-EA comparison reports training accuracy rather than held-out performance. No hyperparameter optimization outside the presented model versions was performed.
record.rows_left_out: No additional distinct results directly bear on a listed version. Minima-flatness profiles and hyperparameter effects described only through figures were not turned into numerical rows because no readable values are stated in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the paired natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets and recovery interventions.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes. Batch-size effects on flatness alone do not test this version.
Dropout's effect on held-out error across data and regularization regimes. Dropout's effect on flatness alone does not test this version.
Magnitude-aware sharpness ranking same-distribution train–test gaps among similarly fitted networks, including comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing high-memorization examples versus equally many random examples and measuring retrained test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels apply to the listed versions. Numerical archetype comparisons cannot be reconstructed from the supplied figure captions. The absence of a transfer advantage is explicitly stated, but it is not evidence that the V7 sharpness–generalization-gap correlation is absent.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and same-distribution test accuracy.
A width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold and its effect on same-distribution test error.
A comparison of convolutional and fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD held-out performance.
Large versus small batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
The effect of adding dropout on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to same-distribution train–test gaps across models.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

rows.baseline: Brittle Narrow and Brittle Wide archetypes; numerical baseline figure-only
rows.value: Authors state flatter-minima models did not seem to generalize better and were more resilient to input noise; numerical values figure-only.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars derived from sampling replicas (Figure 8 caption); numerical uncertainty for Figure 3 not stated in supplied text.
rows.locator: Experimental results, “They are More Robust”; Figures 3 and 15; Appendix Figure 8 caption
rows.note: Related transfer-to-withheld-classes and corruption outcomes; neither measures the same-distribution generalization gap named in the claim versions.
rows.check: Combines transfer accuracy, transfer speed, and corruption robustness, which should be separate outcomes. The authors explicitly report no transfer advantage and greater noise robustness, but neither establishes a listed version. The 9,854 parameter count describes the base architecture, not this wider archetype. Figure 8 error bars concern flatness sweeps and cannot establish uncertainty for Figure 3.
